question: What is the main job of the coronary circulation network?

options.A: Regulate systemic blood pressure via baroreceptors
options.B: Pump deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary arteries
options.C: Filter waste products from systemic venous return
options.D: Supply oxygenated blood directly to the heart muscle

explanation: Even though the heart pumps blood to the whole body, the heart muscle itself needs its own blood supply! Coronary vessels branch off the aorta to feed the myocardium with fresh oxygen and nutrients. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h1)

question: Which part of the heart is usually supplied by the Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery?

options.A: The posterior wall of the right atrium
options.B: The front and bottom walls of the left ventricle
options.C: The interatrial septum and bundle branches
options.D: The apex of the right ventricle only

explanation: You'll hear clinicians talk a lot about the LAD! It is super important because it feeds the front and bottom (anterior and apical portions) of the left ventricle, which does the heavy lifting of pumping blood to the body. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h1)

question: During which phase of the heartbeat does the heart muscle actually get most of its blood supply?
explanation: It's a bit like squeezing a wet sponge—when the heart contracts (systole), the blood vessels get squeezed too tight for blood to flow through easily. When the heart relaxes during diastole, blood rushes in to nourish the tissue! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h2)

question: Why is a very fast heart rate (tachycardia) dangerous for the heart muscle's blood supply?

options.A: It causes immediate closure of the aortic semilunar valve
options.B: It increases total systemic vascular resistance too quickly
options.C: It forces blood backward through the coronary sinus
options.D: It shortens the diastolic phase and reduces perfusion time

explanation: When the heart beats too fast, it rushes through its resting time (diastole). Less rest time means less time for blood to flow into the heart muscle, which can starve the myocardium of oxygen. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h2)

question: How does the heart muscle adapt when it suddenly needs more oxygen, like during exercise?

options.A: It extracts significantly more oxygen from baseline blood flow
options.B: It decreases heart rate to prolong the systolic phase
options.C: It switches entirely to anaerobic metabolism at rest
options.D: It increases coronary blood flow through local vasodilation

explanation: At rest, the heart already takes most of the oxygen it can from the blood. So, to get more oxygen during activity, the coronary blood vessels must widen (vasodilate) to let more blood flow through. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h3)

question: Which natural chemical acts as a powerful vasodilator in the heart's blood vessels?
explanation: When the heart works hard, it releases adenosine. This helpful chemical relaxes the smooth muscle in the blood vessels, causing them to widen so more blood can rush in to help. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h3)

question: What is the underlying process that causes most cases of narrowed coronary arteries?
explanation: Atherosclerosis is the buildup of fatty plaques inside the arteries over time. As these plaques grow, they narrow the pathway, making it harder for blood to reach the heart muscle. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h4)

question: What happens inside heart muscle cells when they don't get enough oxygen during an ischemic attack?

options.A: Increasing baseline oxygen extraction by up to ninety percent
options.B: Halting all electrical depolarization across the cell membrane
options.C: Switching to anaerobic metabolism and producing lactic acid
options.D: Reversing active transport pumps to store excess potassium

explanation: Without oxygen, the cells have to switch to a backup energy plan (anaerobic metabolism). This backup system produces lactic acid as a byproduct, which irritates the tissue and causes that familiar, painful chest pressure. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h4)

question: Which test is considered the gold standard for taking pictures of exact blockages in the coronary arteries?
explanation: During a coronary angiography, a special contrast dye is injected into the blood vessels while using X-ray imaging. This lets doctors see the inside of the arteries clearly and spot any blockages. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h5)

question: A patient comes in with chest pain and high levels of cardiac troponin in their blood. What does this tell you?
explanation: Troponin is a protein found inside heart muscle cells. When those cells get damaged or die, they leak troponin into the bloodstream—acting like a flare signal that heart muscle injury has happened. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h5)

question: How does sublingual nitroglycerin help someone experiencing chest pain from heart disease?

options.A: Vasodilation to reduce cardiac workload and improve perfusion
options.B: Immediate lowering of systemic blood serum cholesterol
options.C: Permanent blockade of sympathetic beta-one receptors
options.D: Direct destruction of existing lipid plaques within arteries

explanation: Nitroglycerin relaxes and widens the blood vessels. This lets more blood flow to the heart muscle while easing the heart's workload so it doesn't need as much oxygen. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a risk factor that nurses try to help patients change?
explanation: Regular exercise protects your heart! On the flip side, smoking, high blood pressure, and a poor diet are major lifestyle risks for heart disease that we educate patients to improve. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h6)
